summary: Describes an EPP mapping for provisioning and managing Internet domain names in a shared central repository, defining command syntax and meaning for domains. It obsoletes RFC 3731. It is a draft standard, replaced by RFC 5731.

eli5.summary: This note says exactly how to ask a registry to create, change, or check a domain name using EPP.

subtitle: Using EPP to manage domain names in a registry system

tldr.problem: Domain registries need a standard way for registrars to create, modify, delete, and check domain name objects. The Extensible Provisioning Protocol provides the infrastructure, but each registry object type (domains, hosts, contacts) needs a specific mapping that defines the XML elements and rules for that object.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4931 defines how to send EPP commands for domain operations: check if a domain name is available, retrieve domain details (registrant, name servers, status), transfer domain ownership, create a new domain registration, renew an expiring registration, and modify domain properties. Each command maps to specific XML elements that describe the domain's attributes.
tldr.outcome: This mapping made EPP practical for domain registrars, but was obsoleted by RFC 5731, which consolidated improvements and aligned with later domain name standards including IDN (internationalized domain names) support. Both EPP and this domain mapping have become standards in domain registries worldwide.

facts.label: Commands Defined
facts.value: check, info, transfer (query), create, delete, renew, transfer, update

facts.label: Contact Types
facts.value: registrant, admin, tech, billing (up to 3 of these)

today: RFC 4931 was obsoleted by RFC 5731 in 2009, which refined the mapping and added better support for internationalized domain names. EPP domain name provisioning is now the standard in domain registries, with RFC 5731 widely deployed. This RFC represents an important transitional step in the evolution of EPP as a provisioning protocol.

sections.title: Domain Objects in EPP
sections.content:
EPP's domain name mapping lets clients interact with a domain name registry as if it were a database of domain objects. Each domain object has attributes such as the fully qualified domain name, registrant contact, administrative contact, technical contact, name servers (delegated hosts), status values, creation date, expiration date, transfer status, and authorization information.

A domain name follows DNS naming rules (RFC 952 and RFC 1123). The mapping assumes domains are stored in a shared central repository and optionally defines a relationship between domains and subordinate host objects. For example, the domain "example.com" may have subordinate host objects like "ns1.example.com" and "ns2.example.com". Domains use either references to host objects in the registry or inline host attributes that include the host name and optionally IP addresses for DNS glue records.
sections.eli5: In the registry, a domain is like a record card with the owner's name, contact information, the nameservers that point to it, and notes about its status. EPP commands let you fill out and update that card.

sections.title: Domain Object Attributes
sections.content:
Domain objects have several standard attributes that the mapping defines. The domain name itself is the unique identifier and must conform to DNS naming. Status values can be set by the client (prefixed "client") or by the server (prefixed "server"), such as "clientDeleteProhibited" to prevent deletion, "clientHold" to suspend DNS publication, or "ok" for normal operation. A domain must always have at least one status value.

Authorization information is typically a password used during domain transfers. Dates and times are in UTC using the ISO 8601 format with uppercase "T" and "Z" characters. The validity period specifies how long the registration lasts (in years or months), and the domain object tracks creation date, modification date, expiration date, and transfer dates. The registrant contact and up to three types of contacts (admin, tech, billing) identify the human or organizational entities responsible for the domain.

Contacts are identified by a server-unique contact ID. Name servers can be specified as references to known host objects in the registry, or inline as host attributes (name plus optional IPv4 and IPv6 addresses). The mapping preserves the original LAN Frame Check Sequence when carrying bridged traffic to maintain end-to-end error detection.
sections.eli5: Each domain record has slots for the owner's ID, when it was created, when it expires, who administers it, who handles technical issues, the nameservers it points to, and what restrictions are in place.

sections.title: EPP Query and Transform Commands
sections.content:
EPP provides six domain commands. Query commands retrieve information: <check> tests whether one or more domain names can be provisioned (are they available?); <info> retrieves full details of an existing domain object; <transfer op="query"> shows the status of a pending or completed domain transfer request.

Transform commands modify the registry: <create> registers a new domain (specifying the name, initial period, name servers, registrant, and contacts); <delete> removes a domain registration; <renew> extends the registration period; <transfer> changes the sponsoring registrar (requires authorization information); <update> modifies domain attributes (adding or removing name servers, contacts, or statuses, or changing the authorization information).

Each command is an XML message with standard EPP wrappers and domain-specific elements. Responses indicate success or failure and return data (like the list of available names from a check command). When offline review is required before completing an action, the server responds with code 1001 and a pending status.
sections.eli5: The commands are like forms: Check asks "is this name free?", Info says "show me this domain's details," Create says "register this domain," Update says "change the nameservers," Transfer says "I own this now," and Renew says "extend my registration."

sections.title: Command Examples
sections.content:
A <check> command lists one or more domain names to test availability. The response indicates whether each is available (avail="1") or unavailable (avail="0") with an optional reason. An <info> command retrieves the full details of a domain, including its status, registrant and contacts, name servers, subordinate host objects, creation and expiration dates, and (if authorized) the authorization information.

A <create> command specifies the domain name, optional registration period, name servers (by reference or inline), and contacts. A <transfer> command includes the domain name and authorization information; the server responds with transfer status (pending, clientApproved, serverApproved, etc.) and the expected completion date. An <update> command uses add/remove/change operations to modify the domain's attributes without replacing the entire object.
sections.eli5: You send XML messages asking the registry to check if "example.net" is free, to show you all details of "example.com", or to add a new nameserver to a domain. The registry replies with XML that tells you what it found.

sections.title: Internationalization and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The mapping handles internationalized domain names through the Punycode representation defined in RFC 3490, which converts non-ASCII characters to ASCII labels that the DNS can store. All XML in EPP is case-sensitive; the mapping examples show the exact case that MUST be used.

The mapping specifies that servers are responsible for defining policies about which domains can be registered, such as requiring registration only within a particular TLD or second-level domain. When servers advertise support for host objects, they MUST enforce that domains use references to host objects rather than inline host attributes; servers that do not advertise host support MUST allow inline host attributes.

Security considerations include using TLS for EPP sessions and relying on client authentication (typically through a certificate or password). The mapping does not define authorization rules beyond the ability to provide authorization information during a transfer; server policies determine access to domain information and the ability to modify domains.
sections.eli5: Non-English domain names work by converting them to ASCII using a special code. The server decides what domain names are allowed and makes sure registrars follow the rules. Communication is encrypted so nobody can snoop on your registration info.
